## Open

### F-762 — A method named declare made lukaot unloadable by bare node, and tap hid it

> _2026-11-18 · core/lukaot · open_

`@feasibleone/lukaot` could not be loaded by bare `node` at all, and every test passed anyway.
`SignalRegistry` had a method named `declare`, and Node's type stripping refuses that name in a
class body: it strips the parameter types and then fails with
`SyntaxError: Unexpected identifier 'declare'` at the method. The whole package was therefore
unloadable in a real run — the framework executes TypeScript by stripping types, not by compiling it
— while `tap` ran the same files through swc and saw nothing wrong.

The symptom was indirect and cost three attempts to place: the framework's graceful-shutdown spawn
test began hanging, because the first framework class to hold the vocabulary was on the boot path
and the import threw where nobody was listening. A five-line probe
(`await import('@feasibleone/lukaot')` and a timer) reproduced it in a second and proved the import
held the boot graph, and a two-line file with one method named `declare` proved the cause.

Renamed to `declareSignal`. The lesson is not "avoid the word": it is that a package whose sources
are executed by Node's stripper is exercised only by a test runner that uses the same stripper, and
tap does not. Any `import` of a package from the framework's boot path needs one run under bare
`node` before it can be believed.

### F-770 — A declared-off capture could not be enabled by configuration

> _2026-11-20 · core/lukaot · open_

The framework's three captures were declared `enabled: false`, and a process that asked for them
with `log.capture.frameworkHttpExchange.enabled: true` recorded nothing at all.
`createCaptureSurface` skipped an entry whose declaration said `enabled: false` **before** calling
`resolve`, so the host that holds the configuration was never asked: the declaration was the last
word, and the operator's flag reached a member that had already returned. The silence was the
expensive part — a capture that does not run looks exactly like a capture whose rung is too cheap to
print anything.

The judgement moved to the resolver. The surface offers every entry and writes only what `resolve`
answers with; `LukaotLog.#resolveCapture` resolves `enabled` the way a log signal's is resolved, so
the configuration has the last word and the declaration is the default it starts from. The
lukaot-level test that pinned the old contract ("a disabled declaration writes nothing even when the
scope allows it") asserted the bug, and now pins the new one instead: the declaration reaches the
resolver, and a host that answers `undefined` builds nothing.

## Resolved

### F-775 — A configured destination kept the process alive

> _2026-11-20 · core/lukaot · resolved_

The UDP sink created its socket without `unref`, so a process configured with a `log.destination`
never exited: the sport realm's test suite finished both flows in 350ms and then waited until tap
killed it at 250 seconds, and the failure read as "timeout" rather than "the run is over". The flush
timer was already unref'd for exactly this reason and the socket was missed — an open handle is
enough to keep the event loop alive, whatever the timer does.

Fixed: the socket is unref'd beside the timer; the sport suite now exits in 4.7s instead of timing
out.

### F-776 — A public return type nobody could name broke a consumer's build

> _2026-11-20 · core/lukaot · resolved_

`core/blong-mock` could not build: `lukaot.ts` exports `mockVocabulary = contribute({...})`, and the
inferred type names `DeclaredVocabulary` from lukaot's `dist/src/declare`, which the package root
does not export — so `tsc` refused to emit the declaration (TS2883, "cannot be named without a
reference"). The `import './lukaot.ts'` line that looked like a hand edit in `types/index.d.ts` was
the emit of `index.ts`'s side-effect import, written before the build failed on the next file; the
missing `types/lukaot.d.ts` is what made it look broken.

The fix is one export: `DeclaredVocabulary` is part of `contribute`'s public contract and was not on
the package root. A consumer that re-exports what it declared cannot emit declarations without it.

Fixed: DeclaredVocabulary is exported from the lukaot root; blong-mock emits its declarations and
builds.

### F-777 — A decision's arm names are identifiers, and an illegal one fails at boot

> _2026-11-20 · core/lukaot · resolved_

A declared decision's arm names are validated as _signal identifiers_ — one camelCase token — so
`no-account` and `one-gender` throw at declaration time ("is not an identifier … never a dotted
name") and the realm fails to load. The message is clear once it appears, but it appears at process
start: `node --run test` reports the whole tap file as failing with "no tests found", because the
platform never got far enough to schedule the group, and the real error is a few hundred lines up
the log. Declare the arms in camelCase (`noAccount`, `oneGender`). A bare-string `decide('x', …)`
skips the check entirely, which is how the same-name mistake can survive until someone converts it
to a declaration.

Documented: arms are camelCase identifiers; both realms now declare their decisions and compile
against the arm sets.

### F-779 — Two silences on one path: the call records and the sink disagreed

> _2026-11-20 · core/lukaot · resolved_

The CI run was red in three packages, six Playwright specs, all of the same shape: the flow page
listed no execution named after the page's own read, and a diagram that is drawn from one was never
drawn. It reproduced locally in each package. The cause was two independent silences on the same
path, and each alone was enough to empty the ledger.

The emitter: the call channel wrote its records through the level API at debug, so a process
configured at info produced no call records at all - and the flow ledger, every execution row and
every diagram are built from those records. The sink: it refused any record that named no declared
signal, which is every record a served request produces, so even a call record that survived the
level was dropped before it left the process. The lesson is that the two halves were each "correct"
against their own note - the sink's rule came from @@D-889, the channel's level from a reading of
D-223 that treated a level as a decision - and nothing tested the join: a unit test of either half
passes, and only a page that reads the ledger end to end notices. The specs that do read it were the
ones CI caught.

Fixed in the same change: the call channel binds its own logger at debug and the write path keeps
call records off the terminal unless log.calls.stdout asks (D-940); the sink and the ingest accept a
record a flow attributes. The three packages' Playwright specs pass locally.

### F-789 — An unresolvable collector exited the process that was logging

> _2026-11-21 · core/lukaot · resolved_

A process whose collector name did not resolve exited: `createUdpWriter` created a `dgram` socket
and subscribed nothing to `error`, so `getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN viewer` thrown onto that event became
an unhandled emitter error and killed the process. It was found by running the suite with the
`release` intent outside a cluster — where `log.destination` names a Service that only exists there
— and it is the exact opposite of what this file documents two paragraphs above the code: a
collector that is missing costs the records it did not receive and nothing else.

A UDP send's failure only ever arrives on that event — the `send` callback sees the local errors,
not a resolution that fails later — so the writer now consumes it. Nothing is retried or queued: the
batch is already lost, the process keeps its terminal, and the next flush tries again.

The trap for a later reader: the `unref` beside it is deliberate and unrelated — an open socket
keeps the event loop alive, which would make every run one that has to be killed — so the two lines
look alike and only one of them may be removed.

Verified in the code: core/lukaot/src/udpWriter.ts:77 consumes the socket's error event, so an
unresolvable collector costs its records and not the process.
